title: Insurance cuts risk elderly hearing help
full_text:
Labor’s proposed health insurance cuts for over-65s risks robbing another cohort of a key avenue of care, after elderly deaf Australians were told as recently as December they should rely on the rebate to ensure they can afford replacements for their cochlear implants.
The government earlier this year announced a plan to wind back the private health insurance rebate for those aged 65 and over in a move predicted to produce $3bn in savings, while staring down backlash from states warning the reform will heap pressure on public hospitals already reaching “national crisis” levels.
Rolling back the Howard-era rebates would mean more than three million older Australians will have to pay hundreds of dollars more for their private health insurance each year from next April and has already sparked warnings of a range of side-effects for other cohorts.
This includes pregnant women and those with chronic conditions relying on “gold tier” coverage.
But The Australian can reveal the policy will also rob other cohorts of a key avenue for care.
After peak bodies representing deaf Australians raised questions over funding for cochlear implant sound processor replacements for over-65s, Health Minister Mark Butler pointed them to that age cohort’s private health insurance rebate – just four months before unveiling the proposal to slash it.
In a December letter from Mr Butler to the Deafness Forum Australia, the minister highlighted that seniors healthcare card holders could rely on the rebate – worth a 28 per cent discount to over-65s and 32 per cent for those 70 and over – to help fund replacements.
“Many private health insurance policies include CI processors under their policies, and I trust that older Australians that undergo CI surgery would consider this avenue of support where possible,” Mr Butler said in his letter to the advocacy body.
Four months later the Albanese government revealed plans to cut the rebate for elderly Australians to 24 per cent, bringing it into line with other age cohorts.
Deafness Forum Australia CEO Rhonda Locke said Labor’s proposed cuts to the rebate would now take those pathways away from vulnerable elderly Australians.
“That seemed to be a legitimate pathway he was suggesting for seniors. Now with that being taken away, we’re really concerned for the 5.5 million Australians we represent, because their pathways are becoming narrower,” Ms Locke said. “We just want to know what the pathway is then – if something is being removed, what is replacing it?” There are about 120,000 Australians with hearing loss who could benefit from a cochlear implant, but only about 12 per cent have accessed the technology.
Ms Locke said reducing the rebate for over-65s risks more Australians lowering their health insurance coverage and missing out on the crucial equipment.
Opposition health spokeswoman Anne Ruston said the revelation was “another example of Labor moving the goalposts on older Australians”.
“On one hand, Labor is telling older Australians to take out private health insurance, while on the other it’s cutting PHI rebates for the very same group. It’s a cynical slap in the face,” Senator Ruston said.
“Many have paid for private health insurance their entire lives, and now when they need it most they’re being told to pay more.” A government spokesperson said that under the proposed changes all Australians will now receive the same private health support based on their income, not age. “Under the proposed changes, over-65s will still receive significant government-subsidised discounts of up to 24 per cent on the premiums private health insurers charge them, the same as the rest of the population,” the spokesperson said. “Labor is investing over $3bn in delivering more aged-care beds, more packages and better care for older Australians through the 2026-27 budget.”
